newsitem.title: CHINA: Hong Kong schoolchildren not amused by handover.
newsitem.headline: Hong Kong schoolchildren not amused by handover.

text.p: Hong Kong schools seem to be having a hard time convincing children to think positively about the territory's return to China, it emerged on Friday.
Children have been calling an opinion hotline to voice misgivings about the historic change of sovereignty.
It transpired that some schools had discouraged pupils from expressing negative views on the switch from British to Chinese flag. At least one child who did said she lost marks on a test.

More than 150 years of colonial rule ended on Monday night amidst lavish celebrations, with China guaranteeing Hong Kong's 6.4 million people they may keep their capitalist way of life unchanged for 50 years and enjoy a high degree of self-rule.
Despite the festivities, many children who phoned in did not welcome the handover, and some were upset that their schools had tried to force them to "think positive".
The hotline run by Hong Kong's Catholic community received almost 200 calls from pupils venting their feelings about the handover. It said 60 percent of the callers were negative.
"One student who did not like the handover drew a picture to show her feelings in class, and her art teacher asked her to change the idea," said Catholic hotline spokesman Kevin Lai.

"Another student said she expressed a negative feeling when answering a test question about the handover, and the teacher deducted 20 marks for her response. But students who held a positive opinion got very high marks," Lai said.
The Catholic hotline, launched in 1995, provides a 24-hour service with a different topic each week and encourages people to express their opinions.
"Schools hold different views about the handover," said Lai.
"Some are very responsive and perform an active role in supporting it. But students who have received a long colonial education may not adapt to such radical change."
Some previously neutral schools now actively promote Chinese patriotism.
At the Lui Ming Choi Primary School in Shatin new town, for example, staff hung up the red flag of China and Hong Kong's new flag and organised the singing of patriotic songs.
"My students are patriotic. I think patriotic education is very important and it's doing well in our school," principal To Lo Ling said. She thinks her pupils will accept the policy.
"No parents have complained so far. When pupils see how patriotic their principal and teachers are, they will follow.
"If any pupils hold different views, teachers should not give them low marks but educate them," she said.
"Primary school pupils are very young. Their patriotic feelings will grow after proper education. Progress may be slow but it will work."
Some parents, however, don't like the idea of teachers trying to stifle their childrens' opinions.
"The changes should not be too fast, but step by step," said the mother of a child in secondary school in Tsing-yi district.
"Children have their own views, schools should not suppress them. I hope my children can receive the same education as before the handover, 50 years no change," she added.
